title: Social Security Design and Its Political Support
text:
The online appendix
This online appendix accompanies Social Security Design and Its Political Support. It extends the paper’s three quantitative sections, on Argentina’s pension reform, on the rich economies with the pension design given and on the endogenous design. It shows the results across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity, the alternative calibration of the taste for leisure, Medicare among the transfers to the old, the UK’s calibration, a second cost of redistribution and the tax rate against a pinned design, the paths behind the paper’s readings in a single year, the UK and France calibrated in full, and the cross-country test under each of its variants. Every number is built by the paper’s own pipeline from the model’s results; none is typed.

title: A. Argentina
text:
Section 5 of the paper calibrates the model with informal households to Argentina before its coverage reforms and reads the reforms as a rise of the universal pension ε; appendix E gives the household survey and the identification. This part shows how the equilibrium depends on the whole pension design, how the reform and the calibration depend on the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES), and what changes when the taste for leisure is identified quartile by quartile.

A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria: the equilibrium in 2010 over a grid of designs (ε, θ), with the reform as a move across it.
A2. The intertemporal elasticity of substitution: the calibration and the reform’s paths in levels at each IES of the grid.
A3. Identification of X: the paper’s common taste for leisure against one per quartile.

title: A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria
text:
Each point of the figure is an economy that has always had one pension design, the universal pension ε on the horizontal axis and the design θ, the weight on earnings-related benefits, in the color, read in 2010 under log preferences; every other parameter is the paper’s calibration. A higher universal pension raises the equilibrium tax rate and lowers the savings rate, the workweek and the savings of informal relative to formal households. A more Bismarckian design lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate and the workweek. The black line is the calibrated θ, and its two markers are the pre-reform ε and the universal level the reform installs. Between them the tax rate rises by more than the reform raises it on impact in section 5: here informal households have always saved under the universal system, while on impact the retirees of 2010 hold savings made under the old one. The rise between the markers is close to the reform’s effect in 2040, once those savings have adjusted.
\(\cdot\)

title: A2. The intertemporal elasticity of substitution
text:
Argentina’s calibration across the intertemporal elasticity
The paper’s benchmark is log preferences, and figure 5.2 reports the reform across the IES ρ. Each ρ is calibrated anew to the same targets, so a change of ρ moves the calibrated parameters as well as the curvature of utility. This page shows both.
Four panels are parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at each ρ, and two are predictions of the calibration, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio in 2010. The discount factor and the political weight of the old both fall as the IES rises. The second falls because the young resist taxation less, so a lighter weight of the old reproduces the observed tax rate. At the lowest elasticities of the grid the thirty-year discount factor exceeds one. The savings rate falls with the IES and the informal savings ratio rises, while the informal productivity and taste for leisure barely move.
\(\cdot\)

title: A3. Identification of X
text:
The calibration
The paper takes the taste for leisure \(X\) common to the four formal income quartiles and pins its level by the average formal workweek, so that relative hours across the quartiles are a prediction. The alternative takes the survey’s relative hours as data and identifies one \(X_i\) per quartile, which leaves the level of hours unidentified. The two calibrations share their targets, \(\beta\), \(\omega\) and every equilibrium outcome of section 5: the tax rate, savings, hours in efficiency units and the reform at every ρ. The reason is that the productivity distribution reaches the aggregates only through \(\sum_{i>0}\gamma_i\eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}\), which both calibrations normalize to one (appendix E). The tables below therefore show only what differs.
Four rows of the paper’s calibration table differ. In the survey, hours rise less with income than the common \(X\) predicts: the top quartile works fewer hours than predicted, and the others a little more. The vector \(X_i\) take those hours as data, so the taste for leisure rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart to reproduce the same relative incomes. The informal productivity and taste for leisure are measured against the formal average and move with it.
\(\cdot\)

title: A3. Identification of X
text:
Why the level of \(X\) differs
The level of the taste for leisure is not comparable across the two calibrations. Under the common \(X\) it is the unit in which hours are measured: it is set so that average formal hours in the model equal the observed workweek, and every productivity scales with it. Under the vector \(X_i\) the survey’s relative hours fix only the ratios of the \(X_i\), and the unit of hours is a normalization, which sets the level of every \(X_i\), of the productivities and of the informal taste for leisure. Since that level enters no aggregate, nothing else moves. Across the IES, the common \(X\) falls a little as ρ rises, because average hours are matched against a slightly different equilibrium at each ρ, while the informal parameters barely move under either calibration.

title: B. Rich OECD countries with the design given
text:
Section 6 of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S. and France and changes the U.S. calibration one characteristic at a time: its pension design, its demography, and the income distribution, voting patterns and taste for leisure that set France apart. Appendix F gives the data and the household heterogeneity of the two. This part shows the calibrations of the U.S., the UK and France across the IES, the U.S. counterfactuals across the Frisch elasticity and the tax rate against inherited savings, what changes when the taste for leisure is identified group by group, the U.S. with Medicare among the transfers to the old, and the UK’s calibration, which the deep test of C6 uses.

title: B1. Calibration
text:
The calibrations across the intertemporal elasticity
Each country is calibrated at every ρ of the grid against its own targets. The discount factor is calibrated on the U.S. and imposed on the UK and France, so their interest factors are predictions. The political weight of the old falls as the IES rises in every country, since the young resist taxation less, and it keeps its ranking: highest in France, then the U.S., lowest in the UK. The savings rate falls with the IES in every country, and the UK’s and France’s interest factors rise toward the U.S. target. The taste for leisure, pinned by each country’s average workweek, falls a little with the IES in the UK and is nearly flat in the U.S. and France. At the lowest elasticity of the grid the thirty-year discount factor exceeds one, which the UK and France inherit.
\(\cdot\)

title: B2. Other parameters
text:
The U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity
The figure shows the counterfactuals of section 6 on the U.S. across the two elasticities that govern the households’ responses. The intertemporal elasticity ρ varies at the paper’s Frisch elasticity; the Frisch elasticity ξ varies under log preferences. At each ξ the U.S. and France are recalibrated to the same targets, so the discount factor, the political weight of the old and the taste for leisure take new values. The ranking of the determinants holds at every ξ of the grid: ageing and the design move the tax rate most, France’s characteristics far less. A higher Frisch elasticity dampens the responses of the tax rate a little and some responses of savings by more, and it enlarges the responses of hours, since labor supply is more elastic, all but that to France’s taste for leisure, which it makes a little smaller.

section: The tax rate and inherited savings
text:
The tax rate and inherited savings
The tax rate of the Markov equilibrium is a function of the state the economy inherits, the savings of the previous period’s young. The figure shows the U.S. tax policy of 2020 at inherited savings below and above their value on the equilibrium path, each IES at its own calibration. Under log preferences the tax rate does not depend on the state (section 3). Away from log preferences it does: at an IES of one half the tax rate falls as inherited savings rise, and at an IES of two it rises, less steeply.
\(\cdot\)

Voters in the Markov equilibrium take this into account. The table gives the size of that strategic term at the equilibrium path, the elasticity of savings to the tax times the slope of the 2050 policy function. It is small at both values of the IES. At one half, a higher tax in 2020 raises the 2050 tax by a small fraction of a percentage point per point, since the policy falls with savings; at two, it lowers it, by less.

title: B3. Identification of X
text:
The calibration
As for Argentina (A3), the paper takes the taste for leisure \(X\) common to the income groups and pins its level by each country’s average workweek; the alternative identifies one \(X_i\) per group from the observed relative hours. In every country the two calibrations share the discount factor, the political weight of the old, the tax rate, savings and aggregate hours. They also share every counterfactual that changes neither the productivities nor the taste for leisure: the design, ageing and France’s voting patterns. The tables and the figure show only what differs.
Two rows of the paper’s calibration table differ, the taste for leisure and the productivity spread. Under the vector \(X_i\) the taste for leisure rises with income in all three countries: observed hours rise less with income than the common \(X\) predicts, the high group working fewer hours than predicted. To reproduce the same relative incomes with those hours, the productivity spread widens.
\(\cdot\)
Group by group, the vector \(X_i\) are a fraction of the common \(X\), and their level carries no information of its own. Under the common \(X\) the level is the unit of hours: it is set so that the model’s average workweek is the observed one, relative to the U.S. for the UK and France, and the productivities scale with it. Under the vector \(X_i\) the relative hours fix only the ratios of the \(X_i\), and the unit is a normalization. That is why the level differs so much between the two while every aggregate is the same.
\(\cdot\)

title: B4. Medicare among the transfers to the old
text:
The calibration
The paper calibrates the U.S. to its public pensions alone, as it does the UK and France: the tax rate covers pension spending, and the design is read off the replacement rates of the public pension (appendix F). Medicare is the other large transfer to the U.S. old. This page reads it as part of the system: its spending enters the tax rate, and since it pays every retiree the same benefit, it enters the design as a flat component. The U.S. system is then larger and less earnings-related than in the paper.
Medicare raises the tax rate by its spending and lowers the design by its share of the transfers, which puts the U.S. design below the UK’s. Both calibrations target the same interest factor and workweek. To hold the interest factor with the larger system the discount factor rises, the political weight of the old rises to sustain the higher tax rate, and the taste for leisure falls a little, at every IES.
\(\cdot\)

title: B4. Medicare among the transfers to the old
text:
The counterfactuals
The figure sets the counterfactuals of the paper’s figure 6.1 on the U.S. with Medicare below those on the paper’s U.S. Ageing moves the tax rate by about as much in the two, and it remains the largest determinant at every IES. Starting from a less earnings-related design, flat benefits raise the tax rate by less and fully earnings-related ones lower it by more; the gap between the two corners narrows, most at an IES of two. France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate by more, and France’s voting patterns raise it by more; at an IES of two, as on the paper’s U.S., France’s voting patterns move the tax rate by more than either corner of the design.

title: B5. The UK
text:
The UK is calibrated as the U.S. and France are in appendix F of the paper, under log preferences, to its own pension spending, demography, design and average workweek, with the U.S. discount factor imposed. Its household data are the Harmonised British Household Panel Survey, wave 17, which refers to 2006–07 and is distributed by the UK Data Service; later waves were collected at least in part during the Great Recession. The income groups are cut as for the U.S., so that the mean incomes of the low and medium groups are half the mean and the mean. The cuts set the population shares and the productivities, not the design: θ is the slope of the public pension on earnings, measured as for every country of the paper’s cross-country test (appendix G.1 of the paper). The propensities to vote are from the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES). B1 gives the calibration at every IES of the grid, and C6 lets the UK’s electorate choose its design.
Table B5.1 sets the UK beside the U.S. and France. Its design is the least Bismarckian of the three, and its population is older than the U.S. one and younger than France’s. Its tax rate is a little above the U.S. one, while its calibrated political weight of the old is the lowest of the three: in the model an older population and flatter benefits both raise the tax rate the electorate chooses at a given weight (section 3 of the paper). The ratio of high to low productivity is close to the U.S. one and well above France’s. The common taste for leisure, pinned by the UK’s average workweek relative to the U.S. one, is the highest of the three, almost twice the U.S. level.

title: C. Endogenous design
text:
Section 7 of the paper lets the electorate choose the design θ as well as the tax rate, under a deadweight cost of redistribution whose parameter λ is calibrated so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. Appendix C derives the cost. This part follows the design along each country’s projected demography, sets the tax rate against a pinned design and a second cost specification against the paper’s, varies the elasticities, reports the checks of the timing of the choice, shows the cross-country test under each of its variants in full, and calibrates the UK and France in full.

C1. The path in levels: the design, the tax rate, savings and hours as the U.S., the UK and France age, with the design chosen and with it pinned.
C2. Other cost specifications: the paper’s cost against a cost attached to the design itself, and the U.S. tax rate against a pinned design, with and without the cost.
C3. Other parameters: the U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity.
C4. The timing of the choice: the corner the design reaches without the cost, under each timing.
C5. The cross-country test: the test of section 7.3 under each variant of appendix G in full, with Luxembourg left out and with the model at the U.S. political weight.
C6. The UK and France calibrated in full: the deep test under the U.S. cost parameter, each country’s own parameter, and the UK’s at every IES.

title: C1. The path in levels
text:
By country
The calibration targets the design of 2020 only; every other design along the path is an outcome of the model, chosen one period ahead. The first two figures follow the three countries from 1990, whose electorate sets the design of 2020, to 2110; the demography is constant from 2080. Each country keeps its own calibration and demography. Its cost parameter is either the U.S. λ, the deep test of C6 along the path, or its own, the parameter at which its electorate re-elects its observed design.
In every country the chosen design moves against the number of workers per retiree. As the population ages, the electorate ties benefits more closely to earnings, and the design levels off when the demography does. Under the U.S. cost parameter the three countries’ designs keep their observed order from 2020 on: the UK’s lowest, France’s highest, the U.S. in between. France’s design stays above the U.S. one, but from 2050 by much less, since France’s population is already old in 2020 and ages least afterwards. The UK’s workers per retiree rise until 2020 before they fall, and its design moves against them, falling and then rising. At their own parameters the UK’s and France’s designs pass through their observed values in 2020 and follow the same patterns. The tax rate rises with ageing everywhere.

title: C2. Other cost specifications
text:
A cost on the design
The paper’s cost of redistribution scales with the size of the system and with the dispersion of relative incomes, so it vanishes when the design redistributes nothing (appendix C). The alternative attaches the cost to the design itself, \(f(\theta) = \phi + (1-\phi)\theta^{p}\), with \(\phi\) imposed and \(p\) calibrated, as λ is, so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. It charges a flat benefit whatever that benefit redistributes. The table gives the two calibrations.

Under the cost on the design, acute ageing raises the chosen design by less at every IES, since that cost does not grow with the tax rate that ageing raises: by about a third as much at an IES of one, the comparison the paper draws, by less still at the lowest IES and by about two thirds as much at the highest. France’s voting patterns move the design further toward flat benefits. France’s income distribution compresses the redistributive stakes but leaves the cost in place, and it takes the design to the Bismarckian corner at every IES.

section: The tax against a pinned design
text:
The tax against a pinned design
The figure pins the U.S. design at one value on the whole path, with the calibration held at the observed design, and reads the tax rate of 2020 without the cost of redistribution and with the paper’s cost. Both lines pass through the calibrated tax rate at the observed design. Without the cost the tax rate falls as the design becomes more Bismarckian, the comparative static of section 3 of the paper: a higher θ shifts benefits from low-income retirees, who with their higher marginal utility weigh more in the political objective, to high-income ones. With the cost the tax rate is hump-shaped in the design, with its peak close to the observed design, which the electorate re-elects. At flatter designs a more Bismarckian one raises the tax rate, since less of the revenue is lost; at more Bismarckian designs it lowers the tax rate, as without the cost. Section 7 of the paper opens with this shape.

title: C4. The timing of the choice
text:
Appendix C of the paper shows that, without the cost of redistribution and at the U.S. calibration, each of the three timings it examines puts the design at a corner. A design chosen together with the tax rate re-splits benefits that current retirees have already earned. A design chosen one period ahead weighs the young’s stake in redistribution against the forward-looking gain of a more earnings-related system. A design chosen once and for all re-splits current benefits and sets future ones at the same time. The table reports the numerical checks, one block per timing. Chosen with the tax or one period ahead, the design is the Beveridgean corner at every IES checked. Chosen once and for all, it is the Beveridgean corner under log preferences and the Bismarckian corner at every higher IES shown.

title: C5. The cross-country test
text:
The paper’s specification
Section 7.3 of the paper tests the model on the countries of figure 1.1. Every country keeps its own workers per retiree, corrected for its gap to the U.S. statutory retirement age, its income distribution, its observed design and its propensities to vote by income group, from the CSES; Luxembourg, which has no CSES survey and enforces compulsory voting, votes at the same rate in every income group. Every country takes from the U.S. the discount factor \(\beta\) and the cost of redistribution as the elasticity \(\varepsilon\), so that country \(n\) faces \(\lambda_{n,t} = \varepsilon\,\Pi_{n,t}/R_{n,t}\) at its own ratio of the pay-as-you-go return to the market return. In the model every country also takes the same political weight of the old \(\omega\), the mean of the weights that match each country’s pension spending at its observed design; the model with each country’s own political weight, own \(\omega\) for short, calibrates each country’s \(\omega\) to that spending. The U.S. anchor, where \(\omega\) and \(\varepsilon\) are calibrated, is measured as every other country is (appendix G.2 of the paper). This page shows the variants of appendix G in full, and the test with Luxembourg left out and with the model at the U.S. political weight.
The paper reports the test in figure 7.2 and table 5, and each country’s own political weight and the design it chooses with own \(\omega\) in table 10. Table 11 gives the slopes under each variant below, and figures G.1 and G.2 the predicted designs.

title: C5. The cross-country test
text:
Other population data
Workers per retiree as the population data give them, and corrected for each country’s gap to the U.S. effective age of labour-market exit in place of the statutory age. The data side of the test does not depend on them. With own \(\omega\) the test hardly moves under either reading, since the political weights are calibrated to spending. In the model the exit age leaves the test close to the paper’s. With workers per retiree uncorrected, Luxembourg, whose population grew fastest, chooses a design close to the Beveridgean corner, and the predicted designs track the observed ones much less closely; without Luxembourg they track them about as closely as under either correction (appendix G.4 of the paper).

text:
The countries outside the test
Figure 1.1, and so the test, leaves out the OECD members before 2000 that the model does not represent. In Korea, Mexico and Turkey a large share of employment is informal, and the model of sections 6 and 7 has no informal households. In Australia, Denmark, Iceland, the Netherlands and Switzerland funded tiers pay a large share of mandatory benefits, or the public pension is tested against them, where the model has a single public pay-as-you-go system. D1 gives the data of the countries the figure covers.

title: C6. The UK and France calibrated in full
text:
The design under the U.S. cost
Besides the U.S., the UK and France are the countries of the paper’s cross-country test with the household data to calibrate the model in full: France in appendix F of the paper, the UK in B5. Each is calibrated under log preferences to its own pension spending, demography and design, with its own propensities to vote, the UK’s households grouped at its own income cuts and France’s at the U.S. income percentiles. This deep test gives each country the U.S. cost parameter λ itself (table 4 of the paper), not the elasticity \(\varepsilon\) that the cross-country test carries across countries (appendix C.2 of the paper), recalibrates its political weight of the old under that cost and reads the design its electorate chooses for 2020. It also calibrates each country’s own λ, the value at which its electorate re-elects its observed design.
Under the U.S. λ both electorates choose designs between their observed ones and the U.S. design: the UK’s well above its observed design, France’s below its own. The three designs keep their observed order, the UK’s lowest and France’s highest, with the U.S. one between them. The U.S. parameter thus reproduces the direction in which each country departs from the U.S. design and part of the distance, a smaller part for the UK than for France. The own parameters rank as the observed designs do, the UK’s below the U.S. one and France’s above it, at more than twice the U.S. value. A higher parameter, under which flat benefits lose more revenue, moves the design away from the Beveridgean corner: the U.S. λ is above the UK’s own and below France’s, and it raises the UK’s design and lowers France’s.

title: D1. The OECD cross-section
text:
Figure 1.1 of the paper sets pension spending and the Bismarckian index of the OECD countries against their population growth and their income inequality. The countries are the OECD members before 2000 in which informal employment is low and one public pay-as-you-go system pays the bulk of retirement benefits. The index is \(I = 1/(2-\theta)\) of the design θ: the earnings-linked share of the least-squares line through the public pension across earnings levels, for men under the rules of 2020 (Pensions at a Glance 2021), times one minus the share of public pension spending on minimum top-ups and tested benefits. Appendix G.1 of the paper gives the rule and the measure. The cross-country test of section 7.3 runs on the same countries, Luxembourg, which has no CSES survey of the propensities to vote, at a flat profile (C5). The tabs below the figure give the values behind each marker with the year each refers to, the provider, dataset and series of every column with the date it was retrieved, and the pairwise correlations the paper’s introduction describes.

title: D2. Numerical checks
text:
The horizon and the terminal condition
Section 4 of the paper computes date-specific Markov policy functions by backward induction along the demographic transition, and tests every candidate equilibrium at each state; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) gives the algorithms. The first table compares the date-specific solution with a time-invariant policy function, the approximation of much of the quantitative politico-economic literature, at the same dates. The second counts, by the solves that wrote them, and the third, for every file of results that records them, the equilibria and the candidates found at any state, and the states at which no candidate passed the test; appendix D of the paper states these counts for the paper’s results. There the solver falls back on a rule of the technical documentation: it ranks the candidate taxes by the integral of the first order condition, and the designs by the political objective with each design at its own consistent distribution of savings. The tables record a fallback only in the choice of the design. A single equilibrium at every state means that the selection rule of section 4 never had to choose.
Appendix D of the paper solves the calibrated economies again with the backward induction started two periods earlier, three periods later and under its steady-state terminal condition, and reports the outcomes in the calibration year and one period later. The table gives the change against the paper’s horizon at every date to the last dated period. Under log preferences the U.S. outcomes do not depend on the horizon. Elsewhere a longer horizon or the steady-state terminal condition moves the tax rate by a few hundredths of a percentage point at most at any date, and the chosen design by less than a thousandth. A horizon two periods shorter moves the outcomes of the calibration year as little, but those of the last dated periods by more, since its terminal period is then close. At the paper’s horizon every date it reports is within a few hundredths of a percentage point of its value under the steady-state terminal condition.

Every table and figure of this appendix is produced by the pipeline in python/paper of the repository, in three stages: the calibrations, the experiments, and a build that reads only their results and writes the exhibits in seconds. REPLICATION.md in the repository maps the data and the code to every output, with the commands and the time each stage takes; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) describes the model, its equilibria and the algorithms. The interactive figures draw from csv files that the build writes from the same results, and each figure’s Data link downloads its file.
